topics.title: Periodic Sequences + Scientific Calculators
topics.text:
One day, NikoIsLife was bored in math class, so he/she was playing with his/her scientific calculator.



NikoIsLife's calculator have the following functions:

- Four basic operations (plus, minus, times, divide)

- Exponents, square roots, $n^{th}$ roots

- Logarithms

- Factorials

- Trigonometric functions (and their inverses)



A function $f(x)$ is called "Casio-able" if it can be expressed using $x$, and only using the functions stated above.



Let $n$ be a positive integer, and $a_1,a_2,...,a_n$ be a sequence of distinct real numbers, where $a_{n+1}=a_1$.



Is it possible to construct a "Casio-able" function $f(x)$, such that $f(a_i)=a_{i+1}$ for all $i=1,2,...,n$?



You can also include other numbers in the function.

This is quite simple if you understand the zeta function, but I wanted to show the "identity" stating $\zeta(-1)=\sum\limits_{k=1}^\infty k.$

Why$\zeta(-1)=\frac{1}{1^{-1}}+\frac{1}{2^{-1}}+\frac{1}{3^{-1}}\dots=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{1}}+\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{1}{\frac{1}{3}}\dots=1+2+3\dots=\sum\limits_{k=1}^\infty k$ $\Box.$

topics.title: Some Probability Problems
topics.text:
These are a few (sort of basic) probability problems that I thought of. Can you solve them? (Note: Please try to give answers as a common fraction, but if needed, you may use a calculator to express the answer as a percent.)



1. Calvin takes a 25-question, multiple-choice test where each question has five possible answers. He answers the first 16 questions correctly. He then realizes that he is running out of time and panics, guessing randomly on the last 9 questions. What is the probability that Calvin scores a 20 on the test?



2a. April's science class has 32 students, including April and her best friend Brooke. April's teacher, Mrs. Palmer, arranges the students randomly into 8 tables of 4, meaning every student has an equal chance of being at any table. What is the probability that April and Brooke will be at the same table?



2b. Mrs. Palmer decides that she will be rearranging the students into the 8 tables of 4 every four weeks. If there        are 36 weeks in the school year, and Mrs. Palmer first arranges the students into tables on the very first day of school, then what is the probability that April and Brooke will be at the same table at least once during the school year?

topics.title: Scary Zeroes 0_0 My Challenge to You
topics.text:
Here is a simple challenge problem, though effectively very, very challenging - a $12$th degree function. This is not a troll! It can really be done by hand! Find the real zeroes of the following function: $$x^{12}-(6-3\pi)x^{10}+(12-18\pi+3\pi^2)x^8+(7-36\pi+18\pi^2-\pi^3)x^6+(3-24\pi+36\pi^2-6\pi^3)x^4+(-3+24\pi^2-12\pi^3)x^2-8\pi^3+1.$$NO WOLFRAM ALPHA!! Please hide your solutions. You are welcome to leave answers in terms of $\pi$.



To spice things up a bit, the first one to solve it receives an upvote. A full explanatory solution must be provided.

topics.title: Burton book problems
topics.text:
Prove that following below :



1) If $a$ is an odd integer, then $a^2 \equiv{1}\pmod{8}$

2) For any integer $a$, $a^3 \equiv{0,1, 6}\pmod{7}$

3) For any integer $a$, $a^4 \equiv{0,1}\pmod{5}$

4) If the integer $a$ is not divisible by 2 or 3, then $a^2 \equiv{1}\pmod{24}$
